candidates.quote: It is not reason never to yield to reason!
candidates.author: Sophocles
candidates.locator: Scene 3, line 570 in the Fitts and Fitzgerald lineation
candidates.speaker: Haimon
candidates.whyThisMonth: A son telling a father that stubbornness is not the same thing as principle: the shortest possible maxim about taking advice, and it fits in one breath before the day starts.

candidates.quote: It is this, let me tell you—that the strongest man in the world is he who stands most alone.
candidates.author: Henrik Ibsen
candidates.locator: Act V, the closing line of the play
candidates.speaker: Dr Stockmann
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last thing said on stage before the curtain, offered to a reader who has to hold an unpopular line at work today and will not be thanked for it.

candidates.quote: When you starts measuring somebody, measure him right, child, measure him right. Make sure you done taken into account what hills and valleys he come through before he got to wherever he is.
candidates.author: Lorraine Hansberry
candidates.speaker: Mama (Lena Younger)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Counsel about how to judge a person you are angry with, handed over at the moment it is hardest to take, which is the moment most readers will meet someone before lunch.

candidates.quote: We live close together and we live far apart. We all go through the same things—it’s all just a different kind of the same thing.
candidates.author: Susan Glaspell
candidates.locator: the one act, Mrs Hale to Mrs Peters (Plays, Small, Maynard and Company, 1920)
candidates.speaker: Mrs Hale
candidates.whyThisMonth: The wisdom of the play in one sentence: that the neighbour you never called on is going through your own trouble in another shape, which is a useful thing to carry into a day of other people.

candidates.quote: Ah, Brother, man’s a strangely fashioned creature / Who seldom is content to follow Nature, / But recklessly pursues his inclination / Beyond the narrow bounds of moderation, / And often, by transgressing Reason’s laws, / Perverts a lofty aim or noble cause.
candidates.author: Molière
candidates.locator: Act One, scene 5, Cléante to Orgon
candidates.speaker: Cléante
candidates.whyThisMonth: The voice of moderation inside a comedy about zeal, warning that a good aim pushed past its bounds turns into its opposite: the counsel an enthusiast needs at six in the morning.

candidates.quote: If you can fill the unforgiving minute / With sixty seconds’ worth of distance run, / Yours is the Earth and everything that’s in it, / And—which is more—you’ll be a Man, my son!
candidates.author: Rudyard Kipling
candidates.locator: closing four lines, Rewards and Fairies (Macmillan, 1910)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most famous poem of counsel in English, and the end of it is the only part that gives the instruction: fill the minute you are actually standing in.

candidates.quote: In seed-time learn, in harvest teach, in winter enjoy.
candidates.author: William Blake
candidates.work: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
candidates.locator: Proverbs of Hell, the first proverb, plate 7
candidates.whyThisMonth: A whole working life laid out in nine words, and it tells a reader which of the three seasons this particular morning belongs to.

candidates.quote: You do not have to be good.
candidates.author: Mary Oliver
candidates.locator: opening line, Dream Work (Atlantic Monthly Press, 1986)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Counsel that arrives as a release rather than an instruction, which is the only kind that lands on a reader who woke up already behind.

candidates.quote: Anyone who has received from God the gift of knowledge and true eloquence has a duty not to remain silent: rather should one be happy to reveal such talents.
candidates.author: Marie de France
candidates.work: The Lais of Marie de France
candidates.translator: Glyn S. Burgess and Keith Busby, 1986
candidates.whyThisMonth: The first named woman poet in French opens her book by arguing that hiding what you can do is not modesty but a failure of duty: an unusually bracing thing to read before work.

candidates.quote: Although the wind / blows terribly here, / the moonlight also leaks / between the roof planks / of this ruined house.
candidates.author: Izumi Shikibu
candidates.whyThisMonth: A thousand-year-old argument that the same gaps which let the cold in are the ones that let the light in, which is counsel for a reader whose life is not weatherproof either.

candidates.quote: Well, son, I’ll tell you: / Life for me ain’t been no crystal stair.
candidates.author: Langston Hughes
candidates.whyThisMonth: The whole poem is advice, and it begins by refusing to pretend the adviser had it easy, which is what makes the rest of it worth hearing at six in the morning.

candidates.quote: Living is no laughing matter: / you must live with great seriousness / like a squirrel, for example— / I mean without looking for something beyond and above living, / I mean living must be your whole occupation.
candidates.author: Nâzim Hikmet
candidates.locator: Part I, opening lines, Poems of Nazim Hikmet (Persea, 1994)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Counsel with a squirrel in it: take the day seriously without treating it as a rehearsal for some better day, which is exactly the temptation at the start of one.

candidates.quote: I got out of bed / on two strong legs. / It might have been / otherwise.
candidates.author: Jane Kenyon
candidates.locator: opening lines, Otherwise: New and Selected Poems (Graywolf, 1996)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is literally a poem about getting out of bed, and it turns the first ordinary act of the morning into the day's first piece of good fortune.

candidates.quote: My candle burns at both ends; / It will not last the night; / But ah, my foes, and oh, my friends— / It gives a lovely light!
candidates.author: Edna St. Vincent Millay
candidates.locator: the complete poem, A Few Figs from Thistles (Frank Shay, 1920)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A four-line aphorism arguing back at every maxim about husbanding yourself, and a month of counsel needs one entry that cheerfully refuses the advice.

candidates.quote: In sandy soil, when deep you delve, you reach the springs below; / The more you learn, the freer streams of wisdom flow.
candidates.author: Tiruvalluvar
candidates.whyThisMonth: From the oldest book of counsel in Tamil, a couplet that makes learning a matter of digging rather than of talent, which is the encouraging version at the start of a day's work.

candidates.author: May Sarton
candidates.locator: opening line, Collected Poems 1930 to 1973 (W. W. Norton, 1974)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Four words that put the whole slow business of becoming who you are in the present tense, on a morning when it does not feel like it has happened yet.
